idiom_name: std::marker traits enforced by the compiler
implementation_notes: Rust's std::marker module is a catalog of marker traits: Send, Sync, Copy and Unpin declare type-level facts with no methods, and the compiler infers them structurally for auto traits or checks explicit impls; generic bounds such as T: Send + Sync then enforce the mark across the program at compile time with zero runtime cost. This is the marker interface absorbed into the language rather than emulated. Implementing an auto trait by hand (unsafe impl Send for T) is an unsafe promise the compiler cannot verify, so reserve it for types that genuinely uphold the invariant.
pitfalls: unsafe impl Send/Sync is a promise the compiler cannot verify; a wrong impl causes data races and is silent.
Auto traits leak negatively: an Rc or RefCell member makes a type !Send/!Sync and can break call sites far away.
PhantomData must name the right type and ownership (PhantomData<fn() -> T> versus PhantomData<T>) or the inferred auto traits change.

variants.name: Hand-written marker trait for user markers
variants.idiom_name: user trait with no items plus explicit impls
variants.implementation_notes: A user-defined marker is a trait with no items plus per-type or blanket impls; because it has no methods anything can implement it, so the mark is only as meaningful as the bounds that consume it, and a private supertrait (sealing) is needed if the set must be closed. Unlike auto traits, a custom marker is not inferred - conformance is an explicit declaration, which is what you want for facts that are decisions rather than structural properties. Prefer it for compile-time capability gates in generic APIs (Deletable, Retryable).
pitfalls: Without a private supertrait seal, downstream crates can implement your marker and change behaviour you believed was closed.
A blanket impl (impl<T> Marked for T) marks every type, including ones you never intended.
Marker traits are not dyn-compatible on their own, so boxing a marker requires a supertrait with methods.
